items.title: China's economy remains broadly stable in October
text: Workers work at a jacquard fabric factory in Nantong, Jiangsu province, on Oct 19. [Photo/Xinhua]
China's economy remained broadly stable in October, with industrial production continuing to expand even as retail sales growth slowed, official data showed on Monday.

The country's value-added industrial output - a key indicator of activity in the manufacturing, mining and utilities sectors - rose by 4.8 percent year-on-year in October, following a 5.5 percent rise in September, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.
Retail sales, a major gauge of consumer spending, increased by 0.4 percent year-on-year in October, following a 1.1 percent gain in September.

Fixed-asset investment - a gauge of expenditures on items including infrastructure, property, machinery and equipment – dropped by 8.1 percent year-on-year in the first ten months, compared with a fall of 7.2 percent in the first three quarters, according to the NBS.
The surveyed urban unemployment rate came in at 5.1 percent in October, down from 5.2 percent in September, the NBS said.
China's economy maintained steady growth in October, the NBS noted, with momentum from new growth drivers intact and the economic structure continuing to improve.

However, the external environment remains complex and volatile, while domestic demand is still insufficient, the NBS said. The bureau noted that some enterprises also continue to face operational difficulties, and more efforts should be made to consolidate the foundation for economic stabilization.

Looking ahead, the country will accelerate the implementation of supportive measures and tap the potential of domestic demand, while optimizing supply and deepening reform and opening-up, the bureau said.
Efforts will also focus on strengthening the vitality of economic development, safeguarding and improving people's livelihoods, and promoting sustained, higher-quality economic growth, it added.

items.title: China's sanctions on politicians of Paraguay and Belize: What do they signal?
text: On October 12, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the People's Republic of China announced countermeasures against Paraguay's Minister of Information and Communication Technologies Gustavo Emigdio Villate Samaniego and Belize's Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca over their Taiwan-related conduct. The measures include freezing their assets in China, prohibiting Chinese organizations and individuals from doing business or cooperating with them, and barring them from entering the Chinese mainland, Hong Kong, and Macao. This is the first time Beijing has sanctioned ministerial-level officials from so-called "diplomatic allies" of the Taiwan authorities. What does the move signal?
A clear message to the other side of the Taiwan Strait: the Chinese mainland holds the initiative in combating "Taiwan independence" separatist forces

Resolving the Taiwan question and realizing the complete reunification is the shared aspiration of all Chinese people. All Chinese people unconditionally support the Chinese government in cracking down on "Taiwan independence" separatist forces and countering foreign interference on the Taiwan question. In September, Paraguayan President Santiago Peña stated in his address to the UN General Assembly that Paraguay is "not neutral" on the Taiwan question, clamoring for Taiwan's "participation" in the United Nations. Prime Minister of Belize John Briceño made similar remarks. From late September to early October, Lin Chia-lung, head of the Taiwan authorities' so-called foreign affairs department, visited Belize and Guatemala. Be it lobbying politicians from "diplomatic allies" to speak up for Taiwan, or making "transit visits" to relevant countries, these moves are nothing but petty tricks by the Taiwan authorities to expand their so-called "international presence" and boast "diplomatic achievements." They can never change the historical and legal fact that Taiwan is part of China's territory, nor can they reverse the historical trend toward China's reunification.

On October 10, Lai Ching-te made a speech to sell the "Taiwan independence" narrative. On October 12, China announced the above-mentioned countermeasures, a clearly targeted move to curb the arrogance of "Taiwan independence" separatist forces and contain the Taiwan authorities' attempt to solicit external support for independence. Experts on international affairs note that China has a wide range of tools at its disposal. When and how these tools are deployed hangs like a sword over the "Taiwan independence" separatists and external forces backing "Taiwan independence."
A warning to Taiwan's so-called "diplomatic allies": China's bottom line and red line must not be crossed

items.title: Together for a bright Asia-Pacific future
text: The 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting will be held in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong province, on Nov. 18 and 19.

As the host economy making its third appearance at the table, China will work with other member economies to chart a blueprint for Asia-Pacific cooperation, focusing on three priorities: openness, innovation, and cooperation.
Together, they will advance the building of an open, dynamic, resilient, and peaceful Asia-Pacific community, injecting fresh impetus into peace and development in the region and beyond.

At the first APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in 1993, a landmark decision was made to move beyond the outdated mentality of bloc confrontation and zero-sum games, deepen economic cooperation and integration in the region, and build a dynamic, harmonious, and prosperous Asia-Pacific community.

Established amid the wave of economic globalization, APEC aims to promote trade and investment liberalization and facilitation, as well as support economic growth and prosperity. It has helped keep the Asia-Pacific at the forefront of global openness and development.

Home to about 40 percent of the world's population, the Asia-Pacific region accounts for more than 60 percent of global GDP and nearly half of world trade, making it a major engine of global economic growth, an anchor of stability for global development, and a hub of cooperation.

In 2020, APEC adopted the Putrajaya Vision 2040, reaffirming its founding mission to improve living standards across the region. The roadmap sets a clear target: to realize an open, dynamic, resilient, and peaceful Asia-Pacific community by 2040.

2026 marks another APEC "China Year." Under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together," member economies are advancing broader consensus on the community's institutional architecture and laying the groundwork for its long-term operational framework.

Sustainable regional progress hinges on enhanced connectivity. Greater openness and seamless cross-border linkages enable Asia-Pacific economies to overcome market fragmentation, deepen cooperative ties, and unlock new avenues for growth.
The APEC Connectivity Blueprint for 2015-2025, adopted in Beijing in 2014, mapped out a path toward a comprehensive, multi-tiered, and multidimensional Asia-Pacific connectivity network.
This year, drawing on the final review of the 10-year blueprint, member economies are developing an upgraded version.

Shenzhen, the host city of this year's APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, is a vibrant city known for its openness and innovation. Where does the vitality of the Asia-Pacific come from? China's answer is innovation.

The Asia-Pacific boasts unique intellectual resources and a well-established tradition of innovation. It has given rise to numerous new technologies, industries, and mechanisms, and has long been at the global forefront of innovation.

Commentary: China, ASEAN have every reason to deepen cooperation
text: MANILA, Nov. 16 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese proverb "a close neighbor is better than a distant relative" also applies to the relations between China and ASEAN, who share an enduring bond and see their cooperation bring tangible benefits to people across the region.
At a time of growing global uncertainties, the two sides have every reason to deepen their partnership, focus on shared interests and keep their cooperation moving forward.

The strength of China-ASEAN relations lies in their shared interests and the practical benefits they deliver. This partnership is too important to be distracted by occasional differences, political rhetoric or external attempts to sow discord.
There is a clear reason for keeping this partnership on track: its benefits are real and far-reaching.

China has remained ASEAN's largest trading partner for 17 consecutive years, while ASEAN has been China's biggest trading partner for six successive years. This year also marks the fifth anniversary of the establishment of the China-ASEAN Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and the 35th anniversary of China-ASEAN dialogue relations, making it an important milestone for taking stock of achievements and charting the way forward.

China has consistently demonstrated its commitment to building a closer China-ASEAN community with a shared future, backing its pledges with concrete actions. With China's participation, the China-Laos Railway has turned Laos from a landlocked to a land-linked nation. Under the China-proposed Belt and Road Initiative, the Sihanoukville Special Economic Zone has made Cambodia a rising manufacturing and export hub. Across Southeast Asia, infrastructure connectivity, industrial cooperation and people-to-people exchanges are creating opportunities that extend well beyond national borders.

Cooperation is also expanding into emerging fields. The implementation of the China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol and closer coordination with the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement will open new avenues for trade and investment. In electric vehicles, digital technologies, renewable energy and green agriculture, Chinese companies are increasingly working with ASEAN partners to develop solutions tailored to regional needs.

Such cooperation is particularly valuable as ASEAN countries seek to upgrade their industries, strengthen economic resilience and move up global value chains. By combining China's industrial strengths, technological capabilities and vast market with ASEAN's dynamic economies and development potential, both sides can create more opportunities for businesses, especially micro, small and medium-sized enterprises.

China's commitment to deeper cooperation with ASEAN also goes beyond the economic arena. It firmly supports ASEAN centrality and ASEAN-led regional mechanisms, and stands ready to work with regional countries to build a peaceful, stable and inclusive regional community.

This year marks the 50th anniversary of the signing of the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation in Southeast Asia. China was the first major country to accede to the treaty, demonstrating its support for ASEAN's principles.

items.title: Cape Verde's Neves secures second term with 63.8% of vote
text: Cape Verde President Jose Maria Neves has secured a second five-year term after winning 63.8 percent of the vote in Sunday's presidential election, according to provisional results from the country's National Electoral Commission.

With 96.8 percent of polling tables counted globally, preliminary results showed Neves securing 63.8 percent of the vote, exceeding the 50 percent threshold required to win in the first round and avoid a runoff.
The 66-year-old incumbent defeated five challengers, including former justice minister Joana Gomes Rosa Amado, the first woman to contest the presidency in the West African island nation.

In remarks to journalists following the release of preliminary results, Neves described his re-election as a "great victory" and dedicated it to the people of Cape Verde, state news agency Inforpress said.
"I dedicate this victory once again to the people of Cape Verde. I am very happy and very satisfied," he said.
Neves, a member of the center-left African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde, served as prime minister for 15 years before becoming president in 2021.
His campaign focused on promoting economic growth, creating jobs for young people and addressing emigration. He pledged to work for higher wages and fight poverty during his second term.
However, voter turnout remained low, with preliminary results indicating that about 68 percent of registered voters abstained, Inforpress said.
The electoral commission registered 419,448 eligible voters, including citizens living abroad. Final results are expected following completion of the counting process.

items.title: Regulatory harmonization key to reviving APEC vision
text: The need to revamp the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific should be a priority at the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, Guangdong province. Member economies should recognize the reality that this long-cherished vision can no longer be achieved through conventional tariff-reduction agreements. A 20th-century border-liberalization approach will not sustain the dynamic economic momentum of the region.

Even though it has no formal negotiating mandate, APEC has successfully reduced average intra-regional tariffs from 17 percent to 5 percent since its inception in 1989. However, border liberalization has reached its structural limit.

Conceptualized by the APEC Business Advisory Council in Hanoi, Vietnam in 2006 and advanced through the adoption of the "Pathways to FTAAP" document by APEC leaders in Yokohama, Japan in 2010, the FTAAP roadmap has passed several milestones, including the Beijing Roadmap in 2014, the Lima Declaration in 2016, the Putrajaya Vision 2040 in 2020 and the Gyeongju Declaration in 2025.

Today, the framework is back on the APEC agenda under China's hosting in Shenzhen. But it returns to a landscape radically transformed by three powerful economic growth engines: digital transformation, the green transition and the intelligent revolution of commerce.

The China-ASEAN Free Trade Area 3.0 Upgrade Protocol, emphasizing the digital economy and green transition, is a crucial prelude to this regional shift. The economic potential in these new sectors is enormous. Southeast Asia's forthcoming ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement alone is projected to unlock a digital market of up to $2 trillion by 2030, showcasing the immense opportunities for the region.

To accelerate regional integration, there is a general consensus on the need to dismantle regulatory fragmentation and make cross-border transactions accessible to and affordable for micro-, small and medium-sized enterprises. Yet, efforts to harmonize digital standards and artificial intelligence governance are hindered by national concerns over data sovereignty and digital security, particularly when geopolitical interests weaponize these issues.
Despite these challenges, the convergence of digitalization, decarbonization and AI presents the Asia-Pacific with an extraordinary opportunity.
Digital trade is poised to democratize global value chains, transcending traditional geographical borders.

Through interoperable cross-border digital frameworks, real-time fintech settlements, paperless customs clearance and digitized logistics, cross-border commerce is no longer the exclusive preserve of conglomerates. It is now within the reach of grassroots MSMEs, which constitute the very backbone of Asia-Pacific economies. The proliferation of e-commerce across the region is creating an inclusive trade superhighway that delivers tangible benefits to grassroots entrepreneurs.

The urgency of the green transition has elevated it from an environmental obligation to an essential component of the energy security hedge on the macroeconomic agenda, highlighted by the recent trade and energy shocks.

items.title: From EV surge to affordable, greener mobility
text: Walk into a car showroom in Melbourne today, and you will notice something that seemed unlikely a decade ago: Chinese electric vehicles are now competing alongside established international brands, offering sophisticated technology at increasingly competitive prices.

For Australian families, this translates to more choices and potentially lower transportation costs. But beyond the showroom lies a broader economic question: could China's EV success create new opportunities for industrial cooperation and shared prosperity across the Asia-Pacific?

As APEC leaders prepare to meet in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, on Nov 18 and 19, this question deserves attention. The future of electric mobility is not simply about which country manufactures the most vehicles, but how economies can strengthen their technological competitiveness and resilience without retreating from international cooperation.

China's achievements in the EV sector are significant. The country has emerged as a global leader through its manufacturing scale, technological innovation, battery expertise, extensive supplier networks and intense domestic competition.

According to the International Energy Agency, China produced nearly 75 percent of the world's electric cars in 2025, with Chinese automakers accounting for approximately 60 percent of global electric car sales.

However, manufacturing strength and technological capability alone do not ensure international commercial success. Ultimately, technology must deliver value that consumers recognize. In a recent study published in the Journal of Business Research, my colleagues and I examined more than 67,000 EV model-year observations from the Chinese market. We found that driving range, a visible technological feature, was positively associated with consumers' engagement with climate-related issues, which in turn was linked to stronger sales performance.
This finding carries an important lesson beyond China's borders: sustainable innovation becomes economically meaningful when consumers recognize its benefits and are willing to embrace it.

For Australian households considering an EV, environmental responsibility is important, but so are affordability, reliability, charging convenience and ownership costs. Sustainability cannot remain an abstract promise. It must deliver environmental benefits while making practical and economic sense.

What holds true for consumers also applies to businesses and international partnerships: technological innovation creates lasting value when environmental responsibility and economic competitiveness reinforce each other, benefiting businesses, consumers and communities.

This is where China's EV success becomes particularly relevant to Australia. Australia has substantial mineral resources and capabilities in research, engineering and renewable energy. China, on the other hand, brings extensive expertise in battery technologies, advanced manufacturing and industrial commercialization.
Together, these strengths create opportunities for mutually beneficial industrial cooperation rather than competition across every segment of the industry.

items.title: Software usability now the focus, say experts
text: Competition in China's smart cockpit market is shifting from adding features to improving how well features work, as large language models are being integrated into more production vehicles.

China's artificial intelligence cockpit solutions market was worth 710 million yuan ($106 million) in the first half of 2026, according to market research company International Data Corporation. IDC forecast the market would reach 1.66 billion yuan for 2026 as a whole and 4.71 billion yuan by 2030, representing a compound annual growth rate of nearly 30 percent.
IDC said newer cockpit AI systems can link functions such as navigation and vehicle controls to handle more complex requests.
SAIC Motor's Roewe brand launched the Jiayue 07 SUV in late October. SAIC said it was the first production model equipped with the Doubao cockpit assistant.

Developed with ByteDance's cloud and AI platform Volcano Engine, the assistant draws on more than 2,000 vehicle service interfaces to handle requests involving navigation, entertainment and vehicle controls, according to SAIC.
The company said the voice assistant will lower the air conditioning and turn down the music if the driver or any passenger says that someone is sleeping.
The range-extended SUV has a starting suggested retail price of 127,800 yuan.
German automaker Mercedes-Benz launched its 2026 long-wheelbase E-Class sedan in early November. The automaker said its China research and development team led the work on the car's AI cockpit.

The virtual assistant uses the Doubao large language model and allows users to operate on-screen controls by voice. It can also recognize users by their voices and remember their preferences, Mercedes-Benz said.
The company said the AI cockpit will receive major over-the-air software updates each quarter and be introduced in other gasoline-powered and electric models.

According to IDC, Volcano Engine held 45 percent of China's AI cockpit solutions market in the first half of 2026, with Alibaba ranking second. Baidu, iFlytek and Shanghai-based artificial intelligence startup StepFun were among other market participants.

IDC said software licensing remains the main way suppliers charge automakers, while some also use fees based on cloud usage or one-time activation charges for in-car software. Some suppliers are exploring car owner subscription fees for AI cockpit services. Roewe said it would cover the costs of AI model use by Jiayue 07 owners.

Chen Qijin, a senior research analyst at IDC China Enterprise Research, said the market remains at an early stage, with its business models and competitive landscape still taking shape. The pace of change will depend on how automakers balance costs and user experience, and whether consumers are willing to pay for AI services, he said.

Wang Chao, a professor at Beijing University of Technology, said automakers should pay closer attention to whether their AI systems complete users' requests reliably rather than to how many features they offer.

items.title: A Chinese Medical Drama’s Remedy for Big-City Blues: Go Home
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019269/A Chinese Medical Drama’s Remedy for Big-City Blues: Go Home
text: A TV drama about a doctor who returns to his small hometown after being fired from a prestigious city-based position has become a hit among young Chinese, who resonate with its message of finding purpose away from competitive urban areas.

“Small Town Remedy” has been hotly discussed since its Nov. 4 finale. Premiering Oct. 21, the show follows Liu Zhengliang, played by A-list actor Xiao Zhan, a young neurosurgeon who returns to his hometown in northeastern China — or Dongbei — from a major hospital following a botched surgery in which his patient dies.

The show’s popularity comes amid a broader shift in attitudes among young Chinese, who increasingly seek a more sustainable work-life balance and self-care amid growing fatigue stemming from relentless competition and conventional definitions of success.

Socially awkward and unfamiliar with local customs, Liu initially struggles to return to life at home after leaving his post in the southern metropolis of Shenzhen. The series depicts how his brother, childhood friends, and former hospital colleagues gradually help him overcome the trauma of his failed operation, among other personal struggles, such as the death of his mother.

Fans have reported being drawn to the drama’s lighthearted tone and the witty humor commonly associated with China’s Northeast, despite tackling heavy subject matter such as illness, death, and grief.

Its popularity has also sparked an online trend of learning the Dongbei dialect, with video lessons gaining traction on social media. One related hashtag — “‘Small Town Remedy’ Dongbei dialect listening test” — had amassed nearly 1.4 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Monday.

The 29-episode drama has earned an average rating of 8 out of 10 on review platform Douban and reached an audience of 148 million across all streaming platforms, according to data from domestic streaming platform iQiyi. Related hashtags on short-video platform Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, had also garnered more than 8 billion views.

Since the show’s finale, online users have been debating what Liu’s next move should be. Some suggest that as a talented young doctor, he should return to a major hospital to pursue better career prospects, while others say he’d be better off staying in his hometown, where he’d have the emotional space to continue recovering and potentially find greater purpose using his medical skills.

“Everyone wants to go to Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen, but if life away from home is too difficult, returning to your hometown is not a step backward, nor is it something to be ashamed of,” one user wrote beneath a post discussing the show on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote. “One’s hometown can be a great choice, too.”

“As urbanization continues, more and more young people are facing the same dilemmas as Liu Zhengliang,” another Xiaohongshu user wrote in a comment under the same post, referring to Liu’s struggles with cultural identity and homesickness. “I think the theme of this show really suits the times.”

items.title: Shanghai Sacks Two Scientists Over Child’s Death in Gene Trial
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019274/Shanghai Sacks Two Scientists Over Child’s Death in Gene Trial
text: Shanghai authorities have dismissed two researchers after an investigation into a child’s death following experimental gene-editing treatment found unheeded safety warnings, failures in ethical review, and undisclosed payments and gifts from the family.

The child had Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, a rare neurodevelopmental disorder with no effective treatment, according to findings released Friday by the Shanghai investigation team. The family contributed 5.3 million yuan ($800,000) toward the research and separately gave researchers approximately 1.06 million yuan in money and gifts.

In July 2023, the family approached Qiu Zilong, deputy director of Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine’s Songjiang Research Institute, hoping his team could develop a customized gene-editing treatment, investigators said.
The child received an injection at the university’s affiliated Xinhua Hospital on March 24, 2025, and died seven days later.
At an emergency review April 2, the hospital’s ethics committee attributed the death to thrombotic microangiopathy, a complication of gene therapy, and ordered the study terminated.

The death went unmentioned in related preclinical research Qiu’s team published in Nature in February 2026, investigators said. The team reported using gene editing to correct a single error in the DNA code of mouse brain cells, restoring levels of a protein essential for normal brain development. The researchers said tests in monkeys also suggested the technique’s potential for use in humans.

Five months later, a joint investigation by Science and Retraction Watch revealed the fatal human trial and reported that the Nature paper had also omitted evidence of liver and kidney damage in animal safety tests.
Shanghai authorities subsequently established a team to investigate the preclinical research, the hospital’s clinical study, and the data underlying the Nature paper.
Investigators found that Qiu’s team had failed to promptly share a safety report from experiments on nonhuman primates with the clinical study’s lead investigator, leaving warning signals unheeded.

Xinhua Hospital’s ethics committee approved the study despite insufficient toxicology and safety evidence, proceeding without additional material it had requested. The hospital also failed to independently and adequately assess the study’s scientific basis and safety.
Investigators said that although the consent form warned the family of serious complications and adverse events, it did not prominently communicate the risk of death.

Investigators found no data fabrication in the Nature paper but identified discrepancies between the research methods used and those described. Data from the same experimental batch had also been presented separately without explanation.

The Nature paper also failed to disclose financial conflicts involving four researchers. Qiu received expensive liquor and electronics worth approximately 100,000 yuan, while Xinhua Hospital associate researcher Yang Kan, the Nature paper’s first and corresponding author, received 900,000 yuan and expensive liquor. Two other members of Qiu’s team each received 30,000 yuan.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: What Made Jade So Valuable in Ancient China and the Americas?
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019256/What Made Jade So Valuable in Ancient China and the Americas?
text: Recent exhibitions at the Shanghai Museum and Beijing’s Capital Museum have introduced Chinese audiences to the civilizations of the ancient Americas. For Chinese visitors, the importance placed on jade may feel familiar. In both ancient China and Mesoamerica, finely worked jade adorned the powerful and accompanied them into the grave, a striking similarity that has long attracted scholarly interest.

How did jade come to carry such authority? One way to explore this question is to compare the jade traditions of Liangzhu and the Classic Maya lowlands, two societies from ancient China and the Americas. Liangzhu was an early regional state near present-day Hangzhou, capital of eastern China’s Zhejiang province, around 3300–2300 BC, with a walled capital, an extensive system of dams, and a pronounced social hierarchy. In the Classic Maya lowlands, spanning parts of present-day Mexico, Guatemala, and Belize, cities ruled by royal dynasties flourished around AD 300–900. Both Liangzhu and Maya cities hold UNESCO World Heritage status.

Thousands of years separated the two societies, and there is no evidence of direct contact between them. Yet both had complex social hierarchies in which powerful ritual authorities played important roles. By tracing jade from the selection of raw stone to its final resting place, we can see how control over labor, knowledge, and materials helped establish its authority in ways that were both similar and distinct.

Jade was valued in both ancient China and the Americas long before Liangzhu and the Classic Maya. The concept of jade encompasses several kinds of stone. Liangzhu’s finest ritual jades were made from nephrite, while Maya jade was principally jadeite. Both were prized for their appearance and could be polished to a lustrous finish. Craftspeople shaped jade using abrasives such as sand mixed with water. Working with different stones helped them recognize differences in hardness and toughness and determine which materials were best suited to particular objects.

In Liangzhu, material choice was closely tied to the form and status of the finished artifact. Other stones, such as serpentine, were generally used for small, less prestigious ornaments. Among the Maya, by contrast, the symbolic meanings of stones were more closely associated with their colors. Green and blue-green evoked water, cultivating maize, and renewed life. Jadeite remained highly prized, but a wider range of similarly colored stones could also be valued for their quality and craftsmanship.
Not everyone had equal access to these raw materials or the specialized skills needed to work them. This inequality helped establish jade’s association with power.

Workshops within and immediately outside Liangzhu city made prestigious ritual objects from nephrite. A short distance away, a large workshop complex specialized in small serpentine ornaments. Despite their proximity, the workshops used different materials and produced different types of objects. The fine finish of these serpentine ornaments, however, shows that their makers were skilled.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: China’s Short Dramas See Quality Shift With AI-Made Historical Hit
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019262/China’s Short Dramas See Quality Shift With AI-Made Historical Hit
text: An AI-generated short drama made by amateurs, including a former rideshare driver and a stay-at-home mother, has gone viral in China for its high production quality and historical accuracy, challenging the genre’s reputation for simple, brainless plots.

First released in August, “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” already has 10 seasons and comprises roughly 1,000 3-minute episodes. As of Thursday, the show has amassed over 12 billion views across platforms including Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, and streaming site Bilibili, local media reported.

In the first nine months of this year, 490,000 micro-dramas were released in China, 13 times more than in all of 2025. AI is also reshaping the micro-drama industry, with AI-generated productions now accounting for more than 90% of all such content, according to a report the National Radio and Television Administration released in October. The report also found that China’s short-drama audience had surpassed 600 million active monthly viewers.

Adapted from a web novel published in installments beginning this April by a writer under the pen name Chagen’er, “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” follows five modern-day soldiers who unwittingly travel back to the late Northern Song dynasty (960–1127), bringing their weapons and military expertise with them.

The late Northern Song period is a popular setting for Chinese time-travel fiction, as it offers viewers an alternative reality to the dynasty’s end, when invading Jurchen tribes captured two of its emperors — widely remembered as a national disgrace.

Fans have praised the drama’s carefully crafted script, elaborate fight scenes, and rounded characters who grapple with everything from the imperial examination system to weapons, food, and military equipment shortages during invasions by northern nomadic groups.
The historical details have prompted some viewers to look up Song-era official ranks, military organizations, and historical records and compare them against the drama’s depictions.

The production team behind “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” reportedly comprises six members — including a former pharmaceutical sales representative, interior designer, rideshare driver, stay-at-home mother, and wholesale business owner — who met during an online course on how to use AI to make short dramas.

Zhang Hansheng, 54, the production team’s head, told domestic media that the series has so far cost roughly 1 million yuan ($150,000) to produce, but declined to disclose the team’s earnings. However, rumors of hefty returns have drawn fresh attention to AI drama production, which many see as a potential source of new opportunities for grassroots content creators.

In the comments on a video interview with Zhang by the domestic outlet Yicai, some viewers said the project had inspired them to learn AI tools and try making dramas themselves. Others urged caution, noting the rise of scams disguised as AI-related courses.

The show’s success comes as the genre shifts toward higher production values. Until recently, short dramas were widely considered mindless entertainment defined by exaggerated interpersonal conflicts, formulaic characters, and implausible plots.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: How ‘Anxious China’ Changed Its Mind About Psychotherapy
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019263/How ‘Anxious China’ Changed Its Mind About Psychotherapy
text: Editor’s note: Zhang Li is a professor of anthropology at the University of California, Davis, and the author of “Anxious China: Inner Revolution and Politics of Psychotherapy,” which explores how a new psychotherapeutic culture is taking root in China amid profound socioeconomic change. A Chinese version of the book was released this summer. Here, Zhang, who grew up in Kunming, capital of the southwestern Yunnan province, talks with The Paper about her personal journey, trends in mental health care, and the potential impact of artificial intelligence.

The Paper: In your book, you say that returning home to Kunming to conduct research into the city’s mental and psychological landscape was a “deeply emotional experience” that sometimes left you feeling vulnerable. How did your personal connection with Kunming shape this project?

Zhang: The idea for the book first came to me when I learned that my best friend from middle school had become a therapist. I was quite surprised. This was around 2000, when interest in psychology was just beginning to take off in China and few people knew anything about mental health counseling. When I talked to my friend about her work, I realized that it touched on all kinds of everyday issues but was relatively unexplored. Most of the anthropological field research I’d come across had been conducted outside China.

As I worked on the project, I discovered how deeply it was connected to my family. My mother died 13 years ago. Looking back, I realized she’d lived with post-traumatic stress disorder for much of her life. She lost her mother when she was 8 years old. Her father remarried, and her stepmother treated her and her siblings very badly.

Growing up, we became accustomed to her extreme emotional reactions, but we had no idea they were symptomatic of a psychological disorder. Back then, people simply described this behavior as having “a bad temper.” It was only after reading up on the subject that I came to understand that my mother had suffered from chronic anxiety and depression, but she lacked the language to express it.

Seeing a psychiatrist is more normalized now; back then, mental health was a taboo topic. When I began my fieldwork, my mother was 80. I repeatedly urged her to see a psychiatrist, and eventually she agreed. After a complicated and rather haphazard diagnostic process, she was prescribed a short course of Prozac, which helped improve her condition. In the final three years of her life, she was relatively at peace, and we could have calmer, more constructive conversations.

I chose Kunming for my fieldwork because it allowed me to leverage personal connections and familiarity with the local environment. In addition, scholars were already conducting similar research in major cities such as Beijing and Shanghai, so I wanted to look at a medium-sized city. Kunming was experiencing many of the same problems as larger cities amid China’s economic reforms and social transformation. Rapid, large-scale change inevitably causes disruption, and the psychological disruption individuals experience manifests in all kinds of ways.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: China’s Hospital Companions Learn Where to Draw the Line
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019255/China’s Hospital Companions Learn Where to Draw the Line
text: SHANGHAI — When prospective clients contacted Li Shuping’s medical companion agency in Shanghai, their first question often had little to do with the hospital visit they were arranging.

“Patients used to ask first whether we were individuals or a legitimate agency,” Li tells Sixth Tone. Patients hire her company, Qingbeihu, to send a trained companion with them to hospital, helping with appointments, consultations, and paperwork.

The agency opened in September 2025, when almost anyone could advertise the same service on social media. And with people aged 60 or older accounting for 23% of China’s population by the end of 2025 and 59 million forecast to need care by 2030, more families were turning to companions to guide elderly relatives through hospital visits.

But written contracts were often absent, leaving services and fees unclear. Some patients faced unexpected charges once a visit was underway, with little recourse if they disputed them, prompting calls for tighter oversight.

But since Shanghai announced new rules for medical companion services effective July 1, Qingbeihu has received more inquiries, Li says. “Orders are growing steadily, and prospective clients seem more willing to trust the service.”

The rules cover medical companion services for Shanghai residents aged 60 and older and set requirements for worker qualifications, pricing transparency, and written contracts. They also require companions to wear identity badges, provide public lists of qualified agencies, and define responsibilities that include helping patients communicate with doctors and offering psychological support.

More recently, a national standard that took effect Nov. 1 covers medical companion services for patients of all ages across China. It also sets limits on what companions can do, prohibiting them from giving medical advice or making treatment decisions on patients’ behalf.

Following Shanghai’s new rules, Li says Qingbeihu now uses written risk and privacy agreements with patients and companions, as well as accident insurance for companions. For elderly clients unfamiliar with digital services, the agency also provides paper consent forms before a visit.
“Elderly people are very willing to have young people accompany them to seek care — it is also a kind of emotional support,” Li says.
For Qingbeihu’s six full-time companions, all under 30, the working day often begins as early as 5 a.m.

By the time Li Suyu, not related to Li Shuping, meets a patient at the hospital around 7:30 a.m., she has already asked about their medical history, drug allergies, and mobility. She then checks registration details and organizes medical records and examination reports before the hospital opens at 8.

Once consultations begin, the 22-year-old accompanies patients to see their doctors, records treatment plans and prescribed medications, and arranges any examinations ordered. She also keeps family members informed and, after the visit, helps patients keep track of follow-up appointments and medication reminders.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019254/Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
text: A pair of Chinese noodle shops serving free meals sparked debate this week after their popularity reportedly disrupted neighboring shops’ business.

“Zero-Yuan Noodle Shop,” which opened two outlets last month in the densely populated Jiangning and Yuhuatai districts of Nanjing, capital of the eastern Jiangsu province, offers only one dish: noodles with braised vegetarian chicken and shiitake mushrooms. Each restaurant has around 50 seats, and since opening have been frequented mainly by middle-aged and elderly customers, according to domestic media.

Jiangning is home to a large migrant worker population, while Yuhuatai has the city’s largest public housing project. Signs outside the restaurants read, “A bowl of pure intention, with no fixed price; three meals a day, offered with warmth to those in need.”

The owner, surnamed Zhang, told domestic media he opened the shops for two reasons: promoting vegetarianism and charity. He said he had previously donated to charities and operated low-cost vegetarian restaurants but found that offering free noodles was the most effective way to achieve his philanthropic goals.

The two shops have served more than 1,000 bowls of noodles each day, Zhang said. He added that he had initially planned to open 10 stores, each serving 500 bowls a day, but demand had exceeded his expectations.
“Our idea was simple: get more people to come eat,” he said.
The topic has garnered more than 10 million views on microblogging platform Weibo, with many questioning whether the measures can genuinely help those in need.

Asked what they thought about the initiative, a local resident told domestic media, “It’s both good and bad. The good thing is that people who are genuinely struggling can come here to get a meal and meet their basic needs. The bad thing is, how can you tell who has money and who doesn’t?”
Other users suggested requiring customers to show their ID cards to exclude locals and help migrant workers.
In an interview with domestic media, Zhang rejected the idea of screening customers. “We want to give people facing difficulties a sense of dignity and respect,” he said.

Domestic media reported that one nearby restaurant’s daily revenue had fallen from 3,000 yuan ($450) to just a few hundred yuan. Another shop owner said he was considering not renewing his lease over concerns about declining customer traffic.

However, some shop owners said customer traffic along the street had already fallen after the relocation of several nearby factories. Others said the free noodle shops had not significantly affected their business.
Zhang told domestic media that affected business owners could work at his stores if they were willing.
He added that the two shops could lose up to 10 million yuan a year. The stores do not have payment QR codes, and he has also turned down donation offers from friends.

The shops have reportedly recently installed barriers to keep lines orderly and stopped providing noodle refills and napkins to discourage those who don’t truly need help from taking advantage of the offer.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: Chip tensions loom over Trump-Xi summit, as US and China push AI safety steps
Suffield Academy scandal highlights ties between New England boarding schools and China
text: Don McMillan, a private school admissions consultant, works with wealthy families from New England to France to Dubai, and helps them gain entry to prestigious boarding schools in the United States and around the world.
But there is one place he absolutely will not work: mainland China.
Why? “The Chinese market,” he said, “is very unique in its value system and expectations.”

This is a delicate way to describe a phenomenon that admissions consultants — and the boarding schools they work with — have  quietly fretted over for some time: how to recruit students and court donors in China while maintaining American standards around conflicts of interest and impartial admissions. The scandal roiling Suffield Academy in Connecticut in recent weeks highlights the reasons why.

Suffield’s longtime head of school, Charles Cahn III, last month went on leave and then resigned amid an IRS probe into his finances. Around the same time, a Suffield board member, Lillian Chen, stepped down. Chen and her husband ran a Chinese company,  XueMei Education, that promised “high net worth” Chinese families that it could “ensure admission” to selective American boarding schools like Suffield, and it repeatedly hosted events with Cahn in China.

There is no public evidence of wrongdoing by Chen or Cahn, and there is nothing inherently dubious about the admissions consulting business, in which families hire consultants to guide them through the application process for elite boarding schools, which can be as hard to get into as — and sometimes serve as pipelines to — Ivy League universities.

But US-based consultants describe a confluence of wealth, financial pressure, demographic trends, and sometimes diverging cultural norms that can make recruiting and fundraising in China especially fraught for American boarding schools.

Like many American colleges and universities, boarding schools are increasingly dependent on international fund-raising, including from China, and on wealthy students from abroad whose parents can pay full tuition, which often tops $80,000 per year.

Schools are contending with a so-called “demographic cliff,” a slump in the number of young Americans passing through high schools and colleges, which may decrease the number of paying customers for private schools.

Boarding schools also face a challenging business model, with high fixed costs and hard caps — in the form of dorm beds and classroom seats — on how many students they can accommodate. Tuition charges have generally outstripped inflation and are now so high that they price out all but the wealthiest Americans — who typically have other private and public school options close to home. Full-pay students can help fund scholarships for less-wealthy students, and international students can make campuses more multicultural and more diverse.
Schools have increasingly looked abroad for students, especially in Asia. And China is the biggest market.

“The thing about China is that you’ve got a relatively small percentage of the population that has extraordinary wealth,” said Neil Chyten, an admissions consultant in Newton. “And they don’t mind spending on education.”
[continua sulla fonte originale]

Trump heads to Asia for 2nd high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi amid Nvidia CEO scandal

items.title: US Reportedly Eyeing Tougher Curbs on China Chip Access
Cantwell urges Lutnick to stop AI chip sales to China ahead of Xi meeting
text: Sen. Maria Cantwell, the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.

In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.

Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.

Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.

"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.

Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act, which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.

She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons, who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."

"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.

Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick to testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: Trump is headed to China this week. Jensen Huang won't be on the trip, but Elon Musk will.
text: Trump is headed to China this week. Jensen Huang won't be on the trip, but Elon Musk will.               Ben Werschkul    · Washington Correspondent  Mon, November 16, 2026 at 5:00 AM EST 4 min read                                NVDA           TSLA           SPCX                           President Trump is set to depart early Monday for a trip to Asia that includes stops in the Philippines and China for meetings focused on trade and other economic issues, but with the ongoing scandal at Nvidia hanging over the journey.

Jensen Huang is not scheduled to be along for the trip, even as Trump continues to voice support for the former Nvidia (NVDA) CEO. But the White House has confirmed that Tesla (TSLA) and SpaceX (SPCX) CEO Elon Musk will join during the China leg at least.
"He's a big part of our national security," a senior US official told reporters, adding that Musk will "be of tremendous benefit just even as an advisor to the president."
Musk is not the only business leader expected to cross paths with the president at a China-hosted CEO summit, one of the major stops of the week.

That gathering is being organized by a group called the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, which announced Sunday that over 100 top global companies — including Apple (AAPL), Google (GOOG), Walmart (WMT), ExxonMobil (XOM), and Boeing (BA) — are set to be represented.
Mastercard (MA) CEO Michael Miebach will be another attendee, the South China Morning Post reported on Sunday, and Chinese state media added that 12 leaders of APEC economies will also attend.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will be on hand throughout the week and has signaled that his focus will be on establishing a new dialogue with China on AI to improve communication.

In a Fox News appearance on Sunday, Bessent raised new questions about what he called a "culture of noncompliance" at Nvidia that led to semiconductor exports potentially ending up in Chinese hands in recent years. He said Nvidia's board of directors should go outside the company for a new executive as part of a "dramatic shakeup."
The summit of business leaders occurs just ahead of an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering being held on Nov. 18-19 in Shenzhen, China

Trump's first stop is a gathering of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in the Philippines that opened over the weekend. The president is set to land in Manila on Tuesday evening, local time.
Trump is expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand as part of those meetings alongside what the White House is previewing as other "commercial deals," one of which is expected to focus on aviation.

Tariffs will be on the agenda for the second half of the trip, when the leaders of the world's two largest economies meet, Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping's third face-to-face meeting of the year. But there is little expectation of major shifts in the relationship.
The White House is previewing the meeting as focused on operationalizing the "Board of Trade" launched earlier this year as both sides search for areas of potential tariff reductions.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: Trump heads to Asia to meet with Xi and Putin amid Nvidia fallout
text:
U.S. President Trump attends a ceremony in honor of Veterans Day at Arlington National Cemetery on Nov. 11  in Arlington, Va.
                
                    
                    Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption
President Trump heads to Asia this week where he's set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian leader Vladimir Putin for a high-stakes trilateral summit.

The trip to China marks Trump's second visit this year, and comes as the president and his party face widespread backlash from voters in the recent midterm elections, potentially weakening his bargaining position across the Pacific.

The president and administration officials – including Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick – are also under scrutiny after the recent resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence officials believe was recruited by China's top spy agency, according to The New York Times. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.
Huang traveled to China with Trump earlier this year – this time, tech billionaire Elon Musk is joining Trump in Shenzhen.
The expectation for major deals or pronouncements coming out of the meetings this week are low – but the meeting is still expected to make waves over the imagery of the trilateral summit.
Before China, Trump will first travel to the Philippines where he'll meet with allies at the ASEAN summit in Manila.
The president is expected to be in the region for just about three days.

For weeks the president has said he's keen to discuss the Iran war and denuclearization with Putin and Xi. But Edgard Kagan, the former ambassador to Malaysia and a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said it's a topic that Xi likely won't want to get into. The White House confirmed Friday that Trump is expected to meet with Xi and Putin together.
"The Chinese strongly disagree with the idea that they should be involved in any kind of trilateral discussions with the United States and Russia on nuclear weapons," Kagan said.

"China wants to avoid this because they don't want to be locked into a subservient position. And they also don't want to create a precedent. I think the main thing for the Chinese is they know if they do a meeting and nuclear issues are discussed, it becomes much harder for them to refuse to do it in the future," he said.
A White House official said they do not expect any agreement to come out of the meeting on denuclearization.
"We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement," the official said, calling the trilateral an "entry point" for the three countries to talk about reducing nuclear weapons stock.
Another U.S. official not authorized to speak on the record acknowledged that denuclearization is a "difficult" topic for China.
"But we do think it's time for China to sort of step up to the adult table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things," the official said.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: A Year On, Mark Carney of Canada Returns to Asia a Political Star
text: The importance of Europe to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s plan to diversify Canada’s economy and politics away from its reliance on the United States was underscored last week by his travel schedule.
Mr. Carney added a stop in Dublin, joining a meeting of European leaders before the start of a previously planned trip to Asia.
Last month Mr. Carney announced that Canada is officially seeking to become the first “associate member” of the European Union. But experts say that Asia offers the greater economic opportunity.

“Prime Minister Carney certainly seems to have a strong focus on Europe, which gives an impression that he is not looking toward Asia,” said Kazuto Suzuki, a professor at the University of Tokyo’s graduate school of public policy. “Nevertheless, if Canada is to avoid dependence on the U.S. market and form a coalition of middle powers, cooperation with Asia is essential.”

Last year, Mr. Carney was something of a curiosity at the meetings of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum. But his speech in January at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, and President Trump’s addition of energy security threats to his trade war with the world have made Mr. Carney and his energy-rich country a marquee attraction at both.

Before the APEC meeting in Shenzhen, China, this week, Mr. Carney will have his second formal meeting this year with China’s leader, Xi Jinping. And Mr. Carney, who is as fond of free trade agreements as Mr. Trump is of tariffs, announced in Manila before the ASEAN meetings opened that Canada had completed the broad negotiations for a deal with the Philippines. Talks are also underway on a wider trade arrangement with all 11 ASEAN countries.

On Saturday, Mr. Carney said that at both summits he would press his call for “middle powers” to unite and would present Canada as a reliable alternative to an increasingly unpredictable United States as a supplier of important products like oil and gas.

“It’s part of our strategy, absolutely, 100 percent,” Mr. Carney said at a news conference after meeting with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. of the Philippines. “We’re very transparent about it. It’s a part of our strategy to develop this dense web of connections to make us resilient, to make us more independent, to make us sovereign so we can live our lives as we choose, so we’re not being told what to do by some hegemon or a hyperscaler.”
“It is to varying degrees part of the strategies of many, many countries,” he added, “and that’s one of the reasons why you’re seeing so much progress.”

Between the Asia summits, Mr. Carney made a quick stop in Cambodia, which is hosting a meeting of the International Organization of Francophonie, an association that promotes French language and culture. There, he received noticeably more applause than anyone else when the leaders were introduced.

items.title: China says Xi-Putin-Trump meeting has ‘groundbreaking significance’
text: BEIJING — China’s Foreign Ministry said Monday that this week’s trilateral meeting between the U.S., Chinese and Russian leaders is of “groundbreaking significance” and will promote world peace and stability.

The meeting between President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin will take place Thursday in China’s southern city of Shenzhen, the site of this week’s APEC summit.

Trump will raise efforts to reduce nuclear arms at the meeting, the White House said last week. China has rebuffed attempts to talk about nuclear arms with Russia and the United States, which have the largest stockpiles of such weapons.

Trump to meet with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping00:50Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters in Beijing this would be the first face-to-face meeting among the three heads of state.
“They will exchange views in depth on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations, which is of groundbreaking significance,” she added.
Under the current circumstances, the three countries bear an important responsibility to cooperate in addressing global challenges and to promote world peace and stability, Mao said.
“Stronger communication among China, Russia, and the United States, along with managing differences and stabilizing relations, serves the interests of all three countries,” she added.
It also meets the expectations of the international community, and helps “stabilize the global situation and advance dialogue and cooperation.”

items.title: US, allies team up to protect AI tech and infrastructure amid China rivalry
The Technology Transforming China’s Factories | Bloomberg Primer
China Doesn’t Want a Nuclear Arms Race
text: LYLE J. GOLDSTEIN is Director of the Asia Program at Defense Priorities and Director of the China Initiative at Brown University’s Watson School of International and Public Affairs.
NINA TANNENWALD is Associate Teaching Professor of Political Science at Brown University.
How America Can Avert an Unnecessary Rivalry

Today, pessimism—almost fatalism—reigns in Washington about the United States’ ability to avoid a costly and dangerous arms race with China. Policymakers point to China’s increasingly aggressive policies toward Taiwan, its massive military buildup, and its resistance to engaging in some arms control measures as evidence that Beijing has accepted the inevitability of such a race or is even pursuing one. Worried by intellectual frameworks that emphasize the likelihood of war between rival great powers, Many U.S. leaders and analysts see little choice but for the United States to arm itself, too. But this thinking risks becoming a self-fulling prophecy. The major danger is that an unrestrained arms race increases the likelihood of war over Taiwan or even of a catastrophic nuclear exchange.

But the pessimism about averting an arms race is misplaced. A nuclear arms race, in particular, is not a foregone conclusion—and the United States has real opportunities to curb one. Avoiding a nuclear arms race will require a broader approach than the two-pronged one Washington has recently favored: building up U.S. nuclear deterrence and seeking to force concessions from Beijing by imposing restrictions on trade and technology transfers. American leaders should instead look beyond traditional deterrence, which falls short because its threat-based approach tends to provoke competition over arms, and strive to establish a more fundamental strategic stability through a process of reciprocal de-escalation and compromise. China is likely to be amenable to reciprocal de-escalation: it has a long tradition of moderation in nuclear matters and, ultimately, Chinese leaders do not want a war over Taiwan.

There are recent signs that even U.S. President Donald Trump, who has often boasted about his distaste for compromise, sees the value of engagement. After two U.S.-Chinese bilateral summits this year, in October he suggested that his November trilateral meeting in Shenzhen with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin should focus on “denuclearization.” But Washington will have to become much more consistent in its rejection of an arms race, including by modifying its support for Taiwan and incorporating China into global arms control leadership. A nuclear arms race with China becomes inevitable only if Washington continues to believe it is.

items.title: Why is China resisting a nuclear treaty with the US and Russia?
text: The world’s top nuclear-armed countries are slated to hold their first-ever trilateral meeting soon as United States President Donald Trump pushes for a new nuclear arms treaty among them.

Trump will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin for talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week in China’s Shenzhen, the White House confirmed.

Top of the agenda for Washington and Moscow is the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), which lapsed in February, marking the end of more than half a century of limits on US and Russian strategic nuclear weapons.
Trump previously rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty, demanding instead a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes Beijing.
But China has long signalled that it is not ready to join any nuclear arms control treaty.

New START was a treaty signed in 2010 by then-US President Barack Obama and Dmitry Medvedev, a close ally of Vladimir Putin who served as Russia’s president from 2008 to 2012. It was extended in 2021 for an additional five years when Joe Biden was the US president.

Under the agreement, Russia and the US were permitted to deploy no more than 1,550 strategic nuclear warheads and a maximum of 700 long-range missiles and bombers, had to impose a limit of 800 intercontinental ballistic missiles in deployment and grant permission for up to 18 inspections of strategic nuclear weapons sites annually by the other party.
New START collapsed in February after the five-year extension lapsed. This key accord was in turn built from earlier arms control treaties signed between Washington and Moscow.

The first of those, START I, was signed in 1991 between the US and the Soviet Union in the dying days of the Cold War. It remained in place until 2009 with the aim of capping US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.

START II, its successor, aimed to further reduce the number of deployed strategic nuclear warheads in addition to removing multiwarhead intercontinental ballistic missiles altogether. It was signed in 1993 but never came into force. Russia formally withdrew from it in 2002.
The Strategic Offensive Reductions Treaty (SORT) from 2003 to 2011, meanwhile, had the same purpose as START I but included less monitoring.

The COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 ended on-site inspections between the two nations in recent years, leaving them dependent on their own intelligence to judge compliance by the other side.
Still, the treaty offered some checks and balances to the two biggest nuclear powers in the world. Together, they possess about 86 percent of all nuclear warheads.
Trump has long wanted China included in the treaty because Washington believes an arms treaty involving only it and Moscow would no longer reflect the global nuclear balance of power.

“Today, the United States faces threats from multiple nuclear powers. In short, a bilateral treaty with only one nuclear power is simply inappropriate in 2026 and going forward,” US Undersecretary of State for Arms Control Thomas DiNanno said in February.
